title: Instrument / condition / moral disposition coincide — no split of disposing vs formally justifying act
source_text: CVIII. Deinde non satis solidum & accuratum videtur, quod distinguunt actum qui disponit ad justificationem, ab eo quem dicunt esse formaliter justificatorium. Nec enim, ex sententia Reformatorum, fides justificat, tanquam forma quaedam per quam justificamur; sed vel ut instrumentum Christi meritum apprehendens, sicut loquuntur multi; vel ut alii non pauci loqui malunt, tanquam conditio foederis gratiae, quam Deus propter Christum ad justitiam imputat. Quae tamen, si accuratius perpendantur, eodem recidunt. Nec enim ullus dixerit fidem esse nostrae justificationis instrumentum Physicum; neque aliter potest hic intervenire fides, quam ut instrumentum morale. Instrumentum autem morale justificationis fidei esse non potest, nisi quatenus Deus credentibus promisit remissionem peccatorum, quam nemo assequi potest, nisi fidei vivae & efficacis interventu. Quod idem plane est, ac esse conditionem foederis gratuiti, quo Deus gratiam & gloriam offert credentibus & resipiscentibus. Similiter fides ad justificationem, non disponit Physice, sed tantum moraliter. Sed dispositio moralis ad beneficium aliquod, non aliud est quam conditio, sub qua illud obtinendum & recipiendum est. Ac proinde fides non aliter justificat, quam per modum cujusdam dispositionis; siquidem eodem hac in parte redeunt, instrumentum morale, dispositio moralis, & conditio sub qua aliquid recipitur. Unde sequitur, hic non esse distinguendum inter actum fidei qui disponit ad justificationem, & inter eum qui formaliter justificat.
pass_a_gloss: Next, it does not seem solid and accurate enough that they distinguish the act which disposes to justification from that which they call formally justificatory. For, on the Reformers’ view, faith does not justify as a form through which we are justified; but either as an instrument apprehending Christ’s merit, as many speak; or, as not a few prefer to speak, as the condition of the covenant of grace which God for Christ’s sake imputes to righteousness. Which, if more carefully weighed, come to the same. For no one will say faith is a physical instrument of our justification; nor can faith intervene here otherwise than as a moral instrument. But a moral instrument of justification cannot belong to faith except insofar as God has promised remission of sins to believers, which no one can obtain except by the intervention of living and efficacious faith. Which is plainly the same as being the condition of the gracious covenant by which God offers grace and glory to believers and the penitent. Likewise faith does not dispose to justification physically, but only morally. But a moral disposition to some benefit is nothing other than the condition under which it is to be obtained and received. And therefore faith does not otherwise justify than by way of a certain disposition; since in this respect moral instrument, moral disposition, and the condition under which something is received come to the same. Whence it follows that here one must not distinguish between the act of faith that disposes to justification and that which formally justifies.
pass_b_english: Splitting a “disposing” act from a “formally justifying” act is not solid.
Reformers: faith justifies not as an infused form, but as instrument apprehending Christ’s merit, or as covenant-of-grace condition God imputes for Christ — which carefully weighed are the same.
Faith is not a physical instrument; only a moral one, because God promised remission to believers through living efficacious faith — i.e., the gracious covenant’s condition.
Moral disposition = the condition under which the benefit is received; so moral instrument, moral disposition, and condition coincide.
Therefore do not distinguish disposing faith from formally justifying faith.
